name: Calcium polystyrene sulfonate
reviewed_by: William Gregory M. Rivero, MD, FPCP, DPSN
drafted_by: AI-assisted draft (Claude) for review by Dr. W. Rivero
summary: Calcium polystyrene sulfonate is a non-absorbed resin that exchanges calcium for potassium in the gut (about 0.7 mmol potassium per gram). The Irish label indicates it for hyperkalemia in acute and chronic kidney insufficiency, including dialysis, so no kidney dose change applies; dosing follows serum potassium. It is not effective enough alone for potassium above 6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes. It has no US FDA label.
kidney_function_basis: Not renally cleared; dose is titrated to serum potassium. Bands shown on creatinine clearance (CrCl).

bands.recommendation: Kidney-indicated drug; dose is set by serum potassium, not kidney function. Usual: 15 g orally three or four times daily (Calcium Resonium SmPC 2024); some products use 20 g 1 to 3 times daily (Sorbisterit). Rectal: 30 g as a retention enema. Stop when potassium falls to 5 mmol/L.

hd.text: Indicated in dialysis patients; same dosing by potassium (SmPC). Not a substitute for dialysis in severe hyperkalemia.

pd.text: Same dosing by potassium (SmPC indication includes dialysis).

crrt.text: Same dosing by potassium only if gut function allows; contraindicated with reduced gut motility or ileus. Colonic necrosis can occur even without sorbitol.

monitoring: Serum potassium (stop at 5 mmol/L). Serum calcium weekly (hypercalcemia, especially with calcium binders or vitamin D analogues) and magnesium. Give at least 3 hours before or after any other oral medicine (6 hours with gastroparesis). Constipation (stop if significant); never give with sorbitol. Colonic necrosis can occur even without sorbitol (SmPC 4.2, 4.4; Harel 2013).

pediatric.approved_ages: Children; not for oral use in neonates (SmPC).
pediatric.usual_dose: Children: 0.5 to 1 g/kg/day orally in at least 3 divided doses; rectal dose at least as large when oral is not possible (SmPC).
pediatric.notes: Neonates: no oral use; no use by any route with reduced gut motility. Fecal impaction after rectal use in children reported.
